summary: Defines a new SMTP reply code, 521, which a host can use to say that it does not accept incoming mail. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo defines SMTP reply code 521 for hosts that do not accept incoming mail. It describes how servers, relays and clients can use the code to stop delivery attempts sooner.

questions: how does a host say it does not accept mail
what does smtp reply code 521 mean
how can a host reject incoming mail
what should an smtp client do after a 521 reply
subtitle: An SMTP reply code for a host that does not accept incoming mail.

tldr.problem: Mail sent to a host without an SMTP server can be queued as a temporary failure, then returned days later with a confusing error.
tldr.mechanism: The host or an MX relay can return SMTP code 521 to state that the host does not accept mail.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1846 is Experimental and was updated by RFC 7504.

today: RFC 1846 is Experimental and was updated by RFC 7504. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why a No-Mail Reply Is Needed
sections.content:
The memo notes that some Internet hosts are dedicated to services such as NTP or DNS and do not provide mail. If a user addresses mail to such a host, a regular SMTP client may treat the missing server as a temporary error and queue the message.

The queued message may remain for days before being returned with a confusing error. Reply code 521 is defined to state that an Internet host does not accept incoming mail.
sections.plainLanguage: A host that has no mail service can be mistaken for a temporarily unavailable mail server. Code 521 tells the sender that the host does not accept mail.

sections.title: Two Ways to Return Code 521
sections.content:
An organization may use an MX relay to bounce mail for a host that does not accept it. The relay may send a 521 reply during the SMTP dialog when the recipient is specified. If a relay of precedence n does this, another relay of lower precedence number for the same host should do so as well.

Alternatively, the host may run a minimal SMTP server that sends an initial 521 greeting. It must then either close the connection or answer commands other than QUIT with 521. If it leaves the connection open, it must time out and close it if the client does not send QUIT; five minutes is suggested.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay can reject mail on the host's behalf, or the host can run a minimal server that replies 521. The memo gives rules for what happens after that reply.

sections.title: Client and Server Rules
sections.content:
A host that sends a 521 greeting must not be listed as an MX record for a domain. The memo says that host is not subject to the postmaster requirement because it does not provide mail service.

If a client receives a 521 greeting from a host in an MX record, it must try another MX host or return the mail with a non-delivery report. If it receives 521 elsewhere in the SMTP dialog, it must return the mail with a non-delivery report.
sections.plainLanguage: A client receiving 521 either tries another listed mail host or returns the message with a failure report. A host that sends the greeting must not be listed as a mail exchanger.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that running no SMTP server, or running one that only emits fixed strings, should provide fewer opportunities for security problems than running a complete SMTP implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says a host with no full SMTP service should present fewer opportunities for security problems.
